title: Drop day · a sketch for HIFI Labs by Juan Pablo García
desc: A launch setup for artist activations on Cloudflare and Firebase, built around the first ten minutes.
h1: Drop day, when every fan shows up in the same minute
lede: An artist posts the link and most of the day's traffic lands in the first few minutes. On Firebase that is a known pain. Google's guidance puts a single document at about one sustained write per second, and says a new collection should start around 500 operations per second and grow from there. This is the setup I would put in front of the next activation, on the stack you already use.
stage: From the artist's post to a live page that holds

flow.label: Diagram of fan traffic going through an edge cache and a waiting room into Firestore

steps.d: The curve is steep. Most fans arrive in the first two minutes, and everything below is built around that shape instead of the daily average.

steps.t: Most requests never reach the backend
steps.d: Pages, artwork and video come from Cloudflare's cache, where you already deploy. Only actions that change something go further.
A Worker hands out signed entry tokens. Fans see their place and a real wait time instead of a spinner and a failed request.

steps.t: Admit at the rate Firestore likes
steps.d: The gate lets fans in on Google's ramp, 500 operations per second to start and 50 percent more every five minutes. A load test the week before warms the same path.
Each fan writes only their own document. There is no shared counter for thousands of fans to fight over.

steps.t: Slow work goes to a queue
steps.d: Claims, receipts and emails run in Cloud Tasks with retries and idempotency keys, so a slow provider never holds up the fan.
One function runs a count query each second and writes a single total. Every fan's listener reads that one document.
